reference.source: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
clinicalPearls: Refers to interposition of the colon (or small bowel) between the liver and the right hemidiaphragm
The radiological Chilaiditi sign is an incidental finding of interposed bowel; Chilaiditi syndrome is the term reserved for when this interposition causes symptoms
Symptoms, when present, are usually non-specific and include abdominal pain, distension, constipation, nausea, and occasionally respiratory discomfort
The key pitfall is mistaking the interposed gas-filled colon for free subdiaphragmatic air (pneumoperitoneum), which can lead to unnecessary surgery
Predisposing factors include a redundant mobile colon, laxity or absence of suspensory ligaments, chronic constipation, cirrhosis, and chronic lung disease
Recognising haustral markings within the subdiaphragmatic gas helps distinguish it from true free air
Most cases are managed conservatively with bowel rest, hydration, laxatives, and decompression, with surgery reserved for complications such as obstruction, volvulus, or ischaemia
reference.pathophysiology: Chilaiditi anatomy arises when a loop of colon, and sometimes small bowel, becomes interposed in the space between the liver and the right hemidiaphragm. This is favoured by anatomical factors such as an elongated, redundant, and mobile colon, laxity or congenital absence of the suspensory ligaments of the liver or colon, a small or atrophic liver, and conditions that enlarge the subphrenic space or increase colonic mobility. When the interposition is merely a radiological observation it is termed the Chilaiditi sign, whereas the syndrome denotes symptomatic interposition, in which distension, altered motility, or occasional volvulus of the interposed segment produces the clinical picture.
additionalDifferentials: Pneumoperitoneum (free subdiaphragmatic air) from a perforated viscus
Subphrenic or hepatic abscess with gas
Right basal lung pathology causing referred discomfort
additionalInvestigations: Erect chest and abdominal radiography noting haustral folds within the subdiaphragmatic gas to distinguish it from free air
Computed tomography of the abdomen to confirm bowel interposition and exclude perforation or other pathology
Clinical assessment for signs of obstruction, volvulus, or peritonitis
Full blood count and inflammatory markers where complications are suspected
Assessment for predisposing conditions such as cirrhosis or chronic lung disease
Contrast studies in selected cases to define colonic anatomy
redFlags: Features of bowel obstruction, volvulus, or ischaemia of the interposed segment
Peritonitis or clinical deterioration suggesting true perforation rather than the benign sign
Intractable pain, vomiting, or distension unresponsive to conservative measures
Respiratory compromise attributable to the interposition
reference.prognosis: The incidental Chilaiditi sign is benign and requires no treatment, and most symptomatic cases settle with conservative management; the outlook is only guarded when complications such as volvulus, obstruction, or ischaemia supervene and require surgery.
pitfalls: Misinterpreting the interposed colonic gas as free air and performing an unnecessary laparotomy
Labelling an incidental sign as a syndrome in the absence of attributable symptoms
Overlooking a genuine complication such as volvulus in a patient with the anatomy
Attributing all right upper quadrant or respiratory symptoms to the interposition without excluding other causes
references: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
management: Distinguish interposed haustrated colon from true pneumoperitoneum to avoid unnecessary surgery, as no treatment is needed for the incidental Chilaiditi sign
Conservative management is the mainstay for symptomatic cases, with bowel rest, hydration and correction of constipation using laxatives and stool softeners
Analgesia and symptomatic relief of distension and nausea, with decompression where required
Identify and address predisposing factors such as chronic constipation, cirrhosis and chronic lung disease
Surveillance for complications including volvulus, obstruction and bowel ischaemia
Surgical intervention, such as reduction, colopexy or resection, reserved for refractory symptoms or complications
